topic: Speech, vision and information extraction concepts

notes.front: In Azure Speech, what is speech recognition?
notes.back: Recognising the words spoken in audio, from a microphone or a file, so that they can be written down as text.
notes.explanation: Out of the box, the recognition model is a base model Microsoft trains on data it owns, so it reflects commonly used spoken language.
notes.example: Like a person listening to a voicemail and noting each word, but done by a model.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech to text?”, “Custom speech” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Out of the box, speech recognition uses a Universal Language Model as a base model. Microsoft trains the base model with data it owns, so it reflects commonly used spoken language.

notes.front: What is speech to text?
notes.back: The Azure Speech capability that converts audio streams into text, in real time or in batches.
notes.explanation: It is the product feature built on speech recognition: audio goes in, a written transcript comes out.
notes.example: Like live subtitles on a television news broadcast, but produced by a cloud service.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech to text?”, “What is speech to text?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Speech in Foundry Tools service offers advanced speech to text capabilities. This feature supports both real-time and batch transcription, providing versatile solutions for converting audio streams into text.

notes.front: What is text to speech?
notes.back: A capability that converts text into humanlike synthesised speech.
notes.explanation: You can use humanlike standard voices out of the box or create a custom voice unique to your product or brand.
notes.example: Like a satnav reading out the next turn, where no one recorded that sentence in advance.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is text to speech?”, “What is text to speech?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Text to speech enables your applications, tools, or devices to convert text into human like synthesized speech. The text to speech capability is also known as speech synthesis. Use human like standard voices out of the box, or create a custom voice that's unique to your product or brand.

notes.front: What is speech synthesis?
notes.back: Another name for text to speech: generating spoken audio from written text.
notes.explanation: Microsoft’s documentation uses both names for the same Azure Speech capability.
notes.example: Like an e-book app reading a chapter aloud, the voice being built as it goes.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is text to speech?”, “What is text to speech?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The text to speech capability is also known as speech synthesis.

notes.front: In speech to text, what is real-time transcription?
notes.back: Instant transcription of live audio, returning intermediate results as the audio arrives.
notes.explanation: Text appears while the speaker is still talking, rather than after the recording ends.
notes.example: Like a typist sitting in a meeting, but the words appear on screen while people are still talking.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech to text?”, “Core features of speech to text” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Real-time transcription: Instant transcription with intermediate results for live audio inputs.

notes.front: In speech to text, what is fast transcription?
notes.back: Transcription of an audio file that returns the result synchronously, faster than real time, with predictable latency.
notes.explanation: You send a recording and wait for the whole transcript in one reply.
notes.example: Like handing a recording to a very quick typist and waiting at the desk for the finished page.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech to text?”, “Fast transcription” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use the fast transcription API to transcribe audio files and return results synchronously and faster than real-time audio.

notes.front: In speech to text, what is batch transcription?
notes.back: Asynchronous transcription of large amounts of prerecorded audio stored in files.
notes.explanation: The work runs in the background, so it suits big collections of recordings rather than live speech.
notes.example: Like dropping a sack of letters at the post office and collecting the replies later.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech to text?”, “Batch transcription” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Batch transcription is designed for transcribing large amounts of audio stored in files. This method processes audio asynchronously

notes.front: In speech to text, what is diarisation?
notes.back: Distinguishing and separating the different speakers in an audio recording.
notes.explanation: It is particularly useful for conversations, meetings and any other audio with several speakers.
notes.example: Like a play script that marks which character says each line, rather than one block of text.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech to text?”, “Diarization” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Diarization is the process of distinguishing and separating different speakers in an audio recording. This feature is particularly useful for transcribing conversations, meetings, or any multi-speaker audio content.

notes.front: In speech recognition, what is a phrase list?
notes.back: A list of specific words or phrases likely to be spoken in the audio, given to the model to guide it.
notes.explanation: It improves accuracy, especially for domain-specific terms, proper nouns and uncommon words.
notes.example: Like giving a note-taker the guest list before a dinner so they spell the names right.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech to text?”, “Phrase lists” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The phrase lists feature allows you to provide the speech recognition model with a list of specific words or phrases that are likely to be spoken in the audio. This helps improve the accuracy of transcription, especially for domain-specific terminology, proper nouns, or uncommon words.

notes.front: What is custom speech?
notes.back: Speech recognition models with enhanced accuracy for specific domains and conditions.
notes.explanation: Use it when the out-of-the-box model is not accurate enough for your domain or your audio conditions.
notes.example: Like training a new receptionist on your firm’s product names, not just everyday English.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech to text?”, “Core features of speech to text” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Custom speech: Models with enhanced accuracy for specific domains and conditions.

notes.front: In text to speech, what is a neural voice?
notes.back: A computer voice produced by deep neural networks, nearly indistinguishable from a human recording.
notes.explanation: With clear articulation, neural text to speech reduces listening fatigue during AI interactions.
notes.example: Like a skilled audiobook narrator, but generated by a model for any text you send.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is text to speech?”, “Neural text to speech features” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Text to speech uses deep neural networks to make computer voices nearly indistinguishable from human recordings. With clear articulation, neural text to speech reduces listening fatigue during AI interactions.

notes.front: What is Speech Synthesis Markup Language (SSML)?
notes.back: A markup language used to customise text to speech output.
notes.explanation: Tags in the text tell the service how to speak it, for example where to pause or how fast to talk.
notes.example: Like stage directions in a script (“pause”, “slower”), but written as tags the voice obeys.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is text to speech?”, “Advanced features” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Speech Synthesis Markup Language (SSML) is an XML-based markup language used to customize text to speech outputs.

notes.front: In text to speech, what is custom voice?
notes.back: A voice you create that is unique to your product or brand, rather than an out-of-the-box voice.
notes.explanation: Custom voice is an umbrella term covering professional voice fine-tuning and personal voice.
notes.example: Like a jingle written for one company, but for the voice that speaks its app.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is text to speech?”, “Custom voice” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: In addition to standard voices, you can create custom voices that are unique to your product or brand. Custom voice is an umbrella term that includes professional voice fine-tuning and personal voice.

notes.front: What is speech translation?
notes.back: Real-time, multi-language translation of audio streams, from speech to speech or from speech to text.
notes.explanation: It works in real time on streams of audio, and across many languages.
notes.example: Like a human interpreter in the booth at a conference, but a cloud service.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech translation?”, “What is speech translation?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The Speech service supports real-time, multi-language speech to speech and speech to text translation of audio streams.

notes.front: In Azure Speech, what is language identification?
notes.back: Identifying which languages are spoken in audio by comparing them against a list of supported languages.
notes.explanation: It can run on its own, with speech to text, or with speech translation.
notes.example: Like a switchboard operator who hears a caller and routes them to the French desk.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Speech?”, “Language identification” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Language identification helps you identify languages spoken in audio by comparing them against a list of supported languages. Use language identification by itself, with speech-to-text recognition, or with speech translation.

notes.front: What is a text-to-speech avatar?
notes.back: A feature that converts text into a digital video of a photorealistic human speaking with a natural-sounding voice.
notes.explanation: The video can be synthesised asynchronously or in real time.
notes.example: Like a newsreader on screen, but the presenter is generated from your script.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Speech?”, “Text-to-speech avatar” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Text-to-speech avatar converts text into a digital video of a photorealistic human speaking with a natural-sounding voice. The video can be synthesized asynchronously or in real time.

notes.front: What is pronunciation assessment?
notes.back: An Azure Speech feature that evaluates pronunciation and gives speakers feedback on the accuracy and fluency of their spoken audio.
notes.explanation: Language learners can practise, get instant feedback and improve their pronunciation.
notes.example: Like a language teacher listening to you read aloud and marking each word.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Speech?”, “Pronunciation assessment” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Pronunciation assessment evaluates speech pronunciation and gives speakers feedback on the accuracy and fluency of spoken audio. By using pronunciation assessment, language learners can practice, get instant feedback, and improve their pronunciation

notes.front: What is computer vision?
notes.back: The AI workload of processing images and returning information about their visual features.
notes.explanation: In Azure it is delivered by algorithms that return information based on the visual features you are interested in.
notes.example: Like a person describing a photo over the phone, but done by software for thousands of photos.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Vision in Foundry Tools?”, “What is Azure Vision in Foundry Tools?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Vision gives you access to advanced algorithms that process images and return information based on the visual features you're interested in.

notes.front: What is Azure Vision (Azure Vision in Foundry Tools)?
notes.back: Microsoft’s Foundry Tool for computer vision. Its product categories are Face, Image Analysis and text reading from images.
notes.explanation: Its algorithms return information based on the visual features you ask about.
notes.example: Like a toolbox with separate trays for faces, pictures and printed words.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Vision in Foundry Tools?”, “What is Azure Vision in Foundry Tools?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Vision gives you access to advanced algorithms that process images and return information based on the visual features you're interested in. The following table lists the major product categories.

notes.front: In Azure Vision, what is Image Analysis?
notes.back: A service that extracts a wide variety of visual features from images, such as objects, brands, faces or adult content.
notes.explanation: It is one of the Azure Vision product categories, alongside Face and text reading.
notes.example: Like a picture librarian who notes what is in each photo, but at machine speed.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Image Analysis?”, “What is Image Analysis?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Vision in Foundry Tools Image Analysis service can extract a wide variety of visual features from your images. For example, it can determine whether an image contains adult content, find specific brands or objects, or find human faces.

notes.front: In Image Analysis, what is a caption?
notes.back: A human-readable description of an image, written in complete sentences.
notes.explanation: The algorithms build the caption from the objects they identify in the image.
notes.example: Like the line of text under a newspaper photo, but written by the service.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Image Analysis?”, “Analyze Image” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Generate a caption of an image in human-readable language, using complete sentences. Computer Vision's algorithms generate captions based on the objects identified in the image.

notes.front: In Image Analysis, what is a tag?
notes.back: A label for a visual feature found in an image, drawn from thousands of recognisable objects, living things, scenery and actions.
notes.explanation: With thousands of possible labels, tags can name scenery and actions as well as things.
notes.example: Like hashtags on a holiday photo, but chosen by the service.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Image Analysis?”, “Analyze Image” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Identify and tag visual features in an image, from a set of thousands of recognizable objects, living things, scenery, and actions.

notes.front: In computer vision, what is a bounding box?
notes.back: The pixel coordinates of a rectangle that marks where an object, person or region sits in an image.
notes.explanation: Several Image Analysis features return bounding box coordinates alongside their result.
notes.example: Like drawing a rectangle around a friend’s face in a group photo before tagging them.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Image Analysis?”, “Analyze Image” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The API returns the bounding box coordinates (in pixels) of each object found in the image, plus a caption.

notes.front: In Image Analysis, what is object detection?
notes.back: Finding objects in an image and returning each one’s label together with its bounding box coordinates.
notes.explanation: It is similar to tagging, but it also says where each tagged thing is.
notes.example: Like a “spot the difference” answer sheet that circles each item it names.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Image Analysis?”, “Analyze Image” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Object detection is similar to tagging, but the API returns the bounding box coordinates for each tag applied.

notes.front: In Image Analysis, what is smart crop?
notes.back: Finding the area of interest in an image that matches a specified aspect ratio and returning its bounding box coordinates.
notes.explanation: The calling application then modifies the original image as it wishes.
notes.example: Like a picture editor choosing the best square from a wide photo for a profile picture.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Image Analysis?”, “Analyze Image” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Analyze the contents of an image to return the coordinates of the *area of interest* that matches a specified aspect ratio. Computer Vision returns the bounding box coordinates of the region, so the calling application can modify the original image as desired.

notes.front: What is optical character recognition (OCR)?
notes.back: Extracting printed or handwritten text from images and documents; it is also called text recognition or text extraction.
notes.explanation: It works on images such as posters and street signs as well as on documents such as forms and invoices.
notes.example: Like retyping a scanned letter into a word processor, but done automatically.
notes.source: Microsoft, “OCR - Optical Character Recognition”, “OCR - Optical Character Recognition” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: OCR or Optical Character Recognition is also referred to as text recognition or text extraction. Machine-learning-based OCR techniques allow you to extract printed or handwritten text from images such as posters, street signs, and product labels, as well as from documents like articles, reports, forms, and invoices.

notes.front: In Azure Vision, what is Read?
notes.back: Microsoft’s OCR engine, which extracts printed and handwritten text, including mixed languages and writing styles.
notes.explanation: It uses several machine-learning models that support global languages.
notes.example: Like a clerk who can read both typed forms and hurried handwriting, in several languages.
notes.source: Microsoft, “OCR - Optical Character Recognition”, “OCR engine” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Microsoft's **Read** OCR engine uses multiple advanced machine-learning models that support global languages. It extracts printed and handwritten text, including mixed languages and writing styles.

notes.front: What is the Azure Face service (Face)?
notes.back: An Azure Vision service with AI algorithms that detect, recognise and analyse human faces in images.
notes.explanation: It supports scenarios such as identification, touchless access control and automatic face blurring for privacy.
notes.example: Like a security guard who checks faces at a door, but as a cloud service.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is the Azure Face service?”, “What is the Azure Face service?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The Azure Face service provides AI algorithms that detect, recognize, and analyze human faces in images. Facial recognition software is important in many scenarios, such as identification, touchless access control, and automatic face blurring for privacy.

notes.front: In the Face service, what is face detection?
notes.back: Finding human faces in an image and returning the rectangle coordinates of their locations.
notes.explanation: It also returns a unique identifier for the stored face data, which later operations use.
notes.example: Like a camera app drawing yellow squares around faces before taking a group photo.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is the Azure Face service?”, “Face detection and analysis” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The Detect API detects human faces in an image and returns the rectangle coordinates of their locations. It also returns a unique ID that represents the stored face data.

notes.front: In the Face service, what is face verification?
notes.back: One-to-one matching: checking whether two faces belong to the same person.
notes.explanation: It matches a face in an image to a single face from a secure repository or photo.
notes.example: Like a border officer comparing your face with your passport photo.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is the Azure Face service?”, “Verification” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The verification operation answers the question, "Do these two faces belong to the same person?". Verification is also a "one-to-one" matching of a face in an image to a single face from a secure repository or photo

notes.front: In the Face service, what is face identification?
notes.back: One-to-many matching: comparing one face with a set of faces in a secure repository to find who it is.
notes.explanation: Match candidates come back ranked by how closely their face data matches the query face.
notes.example: Like a club doorman checking a face against the whole members’ board.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is the Azure Face service?”, “Identification” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Face identification can address "one-to-many" matching of one face in an image to a set of faces in a secure repository. Match candidates are returned based on how closely their face data matches the query face.

notes.front: In the Face service, what is liveness detection?
notes.back: An anti-spoofing check that a user is physically present in front of the camera.
notes.explanation: It guards against spoofing with a printed photo, recorded video or a 3D mask of the user’s face.
notes.example: Like a bank clerk asking you to turn your head, to be sure you are not a photograph.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is the Azure Face service?”, “Example use cases” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Liveness detection is an anti-spoofing feature that checks whether a user is physically present in front of the camera. It's used to prevent spoofing attacks using a printed photo, recorded video, or a 3D mask of the user's face.

notes.front: What is image generation?
notes.back: Creating new images from text prompts, optionally with input images, using an image generation model.
notes.explanation: The prompt describes the picture; an optional input image gives the model something to start from.
notes.example: Like briefing an illustrator in words and getting a picture back, but in seconds.
notes.source: Microsoft, “How to use image generation models from OpenAI”, “How to use image generation models from OpenAI” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: OpenAI's image generation models create images from user-provided text prompts and optional images.

notes.front: What is information extraction?
notes.back: Turning unstructured content, such as documents, images, audio and video, into structured output you define.
notes.explanation: The output can feed automation and analytics workflows directly.
notes.example: Like a clerk who reads a stack of letters and fills in a spreadsheet row for each.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools?”, “What is Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: It uses generative AI to process and ingest many types of content, including documents, images, videos, and audio, into a user-defined output format. Content Understanding offers a streamlined process to reason over large amounts of unstructured data, accelerating time-to-value by generating an output that you can integrate into automation and analytical workflows.

notes.front: What is intelligent document processing (IDP)?
notes.back: Converting unstructured documents into structured data, such as validated fields from invoices, contracts or claims.
notes.explanation: Confidence scores and grounding help keep the data accurate while reducing manual review.
notes.example: Like an accounts clerk keying invoice totals into the ledger, but automated.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools?”, “Content Understanding use cases” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Content Understanding enables intelligent document processing by converting unstructured documents into structured data with high accuracy. Confidence scores and grounding capabilities ensure data quality while minimizing manual review and reducing operational costs.

notes.front: Besides real-time, fast and batch transcription, what is the fourth core feature of speech to text?
notes.back: Custom speech.
notes.explanation: It is the one core feature aimed at accuracy for specific domains and conditions rather than at speed or volume.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech to text?”, “Core features of speech to text” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Batch transcription: Efficient processing for large volumes of prerecorded audio. - Custom speech: Models with enhanced accuracy for specific domains and conditions.

notes.front: What are two uses that suit real-time transcription?
notes.back: Two of: accessibility captions, pronunciation feedback, helping customer service agents, documentation, voice response systems, among others.
notes.explanation: Each needs the words while the person is still speaking.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech to text?”, “Real-time transcription” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Real-time audio transcription for accessibility and record-keeping. - Evaluating and providing feedback on pronunciation accuracy. - Providing real-time transcription to assist customer service representatives.

notes.front: What two kinds of job does the documentation say batch transcription suits?
notes.back: Transcripts, captions or subtitles for large volumes of audio files, and analysing recorded call-centre calls.
notes.explanation: Both involve many stored recordings that can be processed asynchronously.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech to text?”, “Batch transcription” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This method processes audio asynchronously and is suited for: - Transcriptions, captions, or subtitles for large volumes of audio files - Analyzing call center recorded calls to extract valuable insights.

notes.front: Diarisation in the Speech service can identify up to {{c1::35}} different speakers in one recording.
notes.explanation: If the service recognises more speakers than that, it throws an error.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech to text?”, “Diarization” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The Speech service can identify up to 35 different speakers in an audio recording (if the service recognizes more than 35 speakers, it throws an error).

notes.front: For which kinds of words do phrase lists especially help transcription accuracy?
notes.back: Domain-specific terminology, proper nouns and uncommon words.
notes.explanation: Listing them in advance guides the model to recognise and transcribe them correctly.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech to text?”, “Phrase lists” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This helps improve the accuracy of transcription, especially for domain-specific terminology, proper nouns, or uncommon words.

notes.front: Out of the box, speech recognition uses a {{c1::Universal Language Model}} as its base model.
notes.explanation: Microsoft trains this base model with data it owns, so it reflects commonly used spoken language.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech to text?”, “Custom speech” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Out of the box, speech recognition uses a Universal Language Model as a base model. Microsoft trains the base model with data it owns, so it reflects commonly used spoken language.

notes.front: To improve custom speech recognition of domain-specific vocabulary, what do you train the model with?
notes.back: Text data relevant to your field.
notes.explanation: The text teaches the model the words used in your field.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech to text?”, “Custom speech” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Improving recognition of domain-specific vocabulary**: Train the model with text data relevant to your field.

notes.front: In how many languages and locales are the standard (neural) voices available?
notes.back: More than 100.
notes.explanation: They are high-quality neural voices available out of the box, with no training.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is text to speech?”, “What is text to speech?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Standard voices**: High-quality neural voices available out of the box in 100+ languages and locales

notes.front: What are two uses the documentation gives for neural voices?
notes.back: Two of: more natural chatbots and voice assistants, turning e-books into audiobooks, in-car navigation.
notes.explanation: Each puts a natural-sounding voice where a person would otherwise have to record the words.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is text to speech?”, “Advanced features” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can use neural voices to: - Make interactions with chatbots and voice assistants more natural and engaging. - Convert digital texts such as e-books into audiobooks. - Enhance in-car navigation systems.

notes.front: Which text to speech option suits audio longer than 10 minutes, such as an audiobook?
notes.back: Asynchronous synthesis of long audio, with the batch synthesis interface.
notes.explanation: Unlike ordinary synthesis, the responses are not returned in real time.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is text to speech?”, “Advanced features” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use the batch synthesis API to asynchronously synthesize text to speech files longer than 10 minutes (for example, audio books or lectures). Unlike synthesis performed via the Speech SDK or Speech to text REST API, responses aren't returned in real-time.

notes.front: What are two things SSML lets you adjust in synthesised speech?
notes.back: Two of: pitch, pauses, pronunciation, speaking rate, volume, or several voices in one document, among others.
notes.explanation: You can also define your own lexicons or switch speaking styles with it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is text to speech?”, “Advanced features” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: With SSML, you can adjust pitch, add pauses, improve pronunciation, change speaking rate, adjust volume, and attribute multiple voices to a single document. You can use SSML to define your own lexicons or switch to different speaking styles.

notes.front: Can anyone with a Foundry resource start building a custom voice straight away?
notes.back: No. Custom voice has limited access: you apply, and start after access is granted.
notes.explanation: Microsoft limits access for responsible use.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is text to speech?”, “Key features” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: with limited access for responsible use. Create an Azure subscription and Microsoft Foundry resource and then [apply to use custom voice](https://aka.ms/customneural).

notes.front: What do you need to get started with a custom voice?
notes.back: A handful of audio files and their transcriptions.
notes.explanation: The recordings and matching text are the training material for the brand voice.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is text to speech?”, “Custom voice” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: All it takes to get started is a handful of audio files and the associated transcriptions.

notes.front: How is the text to speech feature billed?
notes.back: By the total number of characters in each successfully processed request, including spaces and punctuation.
notes.explanation: Charges apply even when no audio is produced, for example when the voice language does not match the text.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is text to speech?”, “Billable characters” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: billing is based on the total number of characters in each successfully processed request. This count includes all characters/letters, numbers, spaces, and punctuation; regardless of whether audio output is produced.

notes.front: Into how many target languages can the Speech service translate one input in a single call?
notes.back: Two.
notes.explanation: For more output languages you need a multi-service resource or separate translation services.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech translation?”, “Multiple target languages translation” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: the Speech service directly offers the ability for you to translate the input language into two target languages. This enables you to receive two outputs and share these translations to a wider audience in a single API call. If more output languages are required, you can create a multi-service resource or use separate translation services.

notes.front: Standard real-time speech translation can return what kinds of output in the target language?
notes.back: Translated text, synthesised speech, or both.
notes.explanation: You send an audio stream in a specified source language and choose the target language.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech translation?”, “Real-time speech translation (standard)” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Speech translation uses one standard API for real-time translation with text output, audio output, or both.

notes.front: Which two Azure Vision product categories does the overview label “(legacy)”?
notes.back: Image Analysis and OCR.
notes.explanation: Both still appear in the overview table of product categories, marked as legacy.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Vision in Foundry Tools?”, “What is Azure Vision in Foundry Tools?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: [Image Analysis (legacy)](overview-image-analysis.md)| The Image Analysis service extracts many visual features from images, such as objects, faces, adult content, and auto-generated text descriptions. Follow the [Image Analysis quickstart](quickstarts-sdk/image-analysis-client-library-40.md) to get started.| | [Optical Character Recognition (OCR) (legacy)](overview-ocr.md)

notes.front: When will the Image Analysis 4.0 service be retired?
notes.back: 25 September 2028.
notes.explanation: After that date calls to the service will fail, so Microsoft recommends switching to an alternative in its migration guide.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Image Analysis deprecation notice”, “Image Analysis deprecation notice” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The Image Analysis 4.0 service in Azure Vision in Foundry Tools is deprecated and will be retired on September 25, 2028, after which calls made to the service will fail.

notes.front: In Image Analysis 4.0, what does dense captioning add to ordinary captions?
notes.back: Detailed captions for individual objects in the image, each with its bounding box coordinates.
notes.explanation: You can use it to describe separate parts of an image.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Image Analysis?”, “Analyze Image” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Version 4.0 also lets you use dense captioning, which generates detailed captions for individual objects that are found in the image. The API returns the bounding box coordinates (in pixels) of each object found in the image, plus a caption. You can use this functionality to generate descriptions of separate parts of an image.

notes.front: Does tagging only label the main subject of an image?
notes.back: No. It also tags the setting, such as indoor or outdoor, and items like furniture, plants and gadgets.
notes.explanation: When a tag is ambiguous, the response adds hints to clarify its context.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Image Analysis?”, “Analyze Image” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When the tags are ambiguous or not common knowledge, the API response provides hints to clarify the context of the tag. Tagging isn't limited to the main subject, such as a person in the foreground, but also includes the setting (indoor or outdoor), furniture, tools, plants, animals, accessories, gadgets, and so on.

notes.front: Besides locating objects, what else does object detection tell you that plain tagging does not?
notes.back: When there are several instances of the same tag in an image.
notes.explanation: Each instance gets its own coordinates, so you can process relationships between objects.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Image Analysis?”, “Analyze Image” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can use this functionality to process further relationships between the objects in an image. It also lets you know when there are multiple instances of the same tag in an image.

notes.front: What does people detection in Image Analysis 4.0 return for each person found?
notes.back: A bounding box and a confidence score.
notes.explanation: It is one of the features that version 4.0 added.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Image Analysis?”, “Analyze Image” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Version 4.0 of Image Analysis offers the ability to detect people appearing in images. The API returns the bounding box coordinates of each detected person, along with a confidence score.

notes.front: What do the Image Analysis multimodal embeddings let you do?
notes.back: Search a set of images with a text query, matching by meaning rather than by tags or other metadata.
notes.explanation: Images and text are converted to vectors and matched on semantic closeness, which often gives better search results.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Image Analysis?”, “Multimodal embeddings (v4.0 only)” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Then, you can convert incoming text queries to vectors, and match images to the text based on semantic closeness. This capability lets you search a set of images by using text, without needing to use image tags or other metadata. Semantic closeness often produces better results in search.

notes.front: In what units is OCR text typically extracted?
notes.back: Words, text lines, and paragraphs or text blocks.
notes.explanation: This gives a digital version of the scanned text, reducing or removing manual data entry.
notes.source: Microsoft, “OCR - Optical Character Recognition”, “OCR - Optical Character Recognition” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The text is typically extracted as words, text lines, and paragraphs or text blocks, enabling access to digital version of the scanned text. This capability eliminates or significantly reduces the need for manual data entry.

notes.front: Where can you run the Read OCR engine?
notes.back: As a cloud service or as an on-premises container.
notes.explanation: The container option lets the engine run in your own environment.
notes.source: Microsoft, “OCR - Optical Character Recognition”, “OCR engine” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can use **Read** as a cloud service or as an on-premises container for flexible deployment.

notes.front: Which Face operation is required as the first step in all other Face scenarios?
notes.back: Face detection.
notes.explanation: Detection returns the identifier of the stored face data that later identify or verify operations use.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is the Azure Face service?”, “Face detection and analysis” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Face detection is required as a first step in all the other scenarios. The Detect API detects human faces in an image and returns the rectangle coordinates of their locations. It also returns a unique ID that represents the stored face data. This is used in later operations to identify or verify faces.

notes.front: Are the optional face attributes, such as age or emotion, actual classifications of the person?
notes.back: No. They are general predictions, not actual classifications.
notes.explanation: Some help to check that the app is getting high-quality face data when users enrol.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is the Azure Face service?”, “Face detection and analysis” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Optionally, face detection can extract a set of face-related attributes, such as head pose, age, emotion, facial hair, and glasses. These attributes are general predictions, not actual classifications. Some attributes are useful to ensure that your application is getting high-quality face data when users add themselves to a Face service.

notes.front: What inputs do the gpt-image series models accept, and what do they output?
notes.back: Text and image inputs; they output images.
notes.explanation: This holds across the gpt-image models in Microsoft’s comparison table.
notes.source: Microsoft, “How to use image generation models from OpenAI”, “Models and capabilities” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Accepts **text + image** inputs; outputs images.

notes.front: What four kinds of input can Microsoft’s information extraction service process?
notes.back: Documents, images, video and audio.
notes.explanation: One service handles every modality and produces output in the format you define.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools?”, “Key components of Content Understanding” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The source content that Content Understanding processes. Supports multiple modalities including Documents, Images, Video, and Audio.

notes.front: When extracting content from audio and video, what does the service do?
notes.back: It transcribes the speech and identifies key visual elements.
notes.explanation: For documents it instead extracts text with OCR and recognises layout such as tables.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools?”, “Key components of Content Understanding” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Extracts text using optical character recognition (OCR), identifies selection marks and barcodes, detects formulas, and recognizes layout elements like paragraphs, sections, and tables. For audio and video, transcribes speech and identifies key visual elements.

notes.front: What are two examples of intelligent document processing given in the documentation?
notes.back: Two of: invoice processing, contract analysis, claims management.
notes.explanation: Each extracts and validates fields from complex documents.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools?”, “Content Understanding use cases” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For example, automate invoice processing, contract analysis, and claims management by extracting and validating fields from complex documents.

notes.front: A broadcaster wants subtitles for 20,000 old programmes stored as audio files. Which speech to text option fits best?
notes.back: Batch transcription.
notes.choices:
A) Real-time transcription
B) Batch transcription
C) Fast transcription
D) Custom speech
notes.choicesExplained: A is for live audio as it is spoken. C returns one file’s transcript quickly and synchronously, not bulk jobs. D improves accuracy for a domain; it is not a way of processing volume.
notes.explanation: Batch transcription processes large volumes of stored audio asynchronously.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech to text?”, “Batch transcription” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Transcriptions, captions, or subtitles for large volumes of audio files

notes.front: A lecturer wants captions to appear on screen while she is speaking. Which option fits?
notes.back: Real-time transcription.
notes.choices:
A) Batch transcription
B) Real-time transcription
C) Speech synthesis
D) Diarisation
notes.choicesExplained: A works asynchronously on stored files. C turns text into speech, the opposite direction. D separates speakers but is not itself a transcription mode.
notes.explanation: Real-time transcription returns intermediate results for live audio input.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech to text?”, “Core features of speech to text” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Real-time transcription: Instant transcription with intermediate results for live audio inputs.

notes.front: Minutes of a board meeting must show which director said each sentence. Which speech to text feature provides this?
notes.back: Diarisation.
notes.choices:
A) Phrase list
B) Language identification
C) Diarisation
D) Custom voice
notes.choicesExplained: A improves recognition of listed words. B works out which language is spoken. D is a text to speech voice, not transcription.
notes.explanation: Diarisation distinguishes and separates the different speakers in a recording.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech to text?”, “Diarization” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Diarization is the process of distinguishing and separating different speakers in an audio recording.

notes.front: A pharmacy’s transcripts keep misspelling a few drug names the base model has rarely heard. What is the lightest fix?
notes.back: Add the names in a phrase list.
notes.choices:
A) Add the names in a phrase list
B) Create a custom voice
C) Turn on diarisation
D) Mark up the text with SSML
notes.choicesExplained: B changes how synthesised speech sounds, not recognition. C separates speakers. D controls text to speech output, not transcription.
notes.explanation: A phrase list guides the model to recognise listed words, including uncommon words and proper nouns.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech to text?”, “Phrase lists” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: By using phrase lists, you can guide the model to better recognize and transcribe these terms correctly.

notes.front: A bank wants its chatbot to answer customers aloud in a natural voice. Which capability does it need?
notes.back: Speech synthesis (text to speech).
notes.choices:
A) Speech recognition
B) Speech synthesis (text to speech)
C) Speech translation
D) Pronunciation assessment
notes.choicesExplained: A converts speech to text, the opposite direction. C translates between languages. D grades a speaker’s pronunciation.
notes.explanation: Speech synthesis turns the chatbot’s text replies into humanlike speech.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is text to speech?”, “What is text to speech?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Text to speech enables your applications, tools, or devices to convert text into human like synthesized speech.

notes.front: A museum audio guide must pause for two seconds after each exhibit name and speak dates more slowly. What should the developer use?
notes.back: SSML.
notes.choices:
A) A phrase list
B) SSML
C) Custom speech
D) Diarisation
notes.choicesExplained: A and C improve recognition of speech, not how speech is produced. D separates speakers in a recording.
notes.explanation: SSML lets you add pauses and change the speaking rate of synthesised speech.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is text to speech?”, “Advanced features” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: With SSML, you can adjust pitch, add pauses, improve pronunciation, change speaking rate, adjust volume

notes.front: A tour guide speaks Italian and visitors must hear her in English through earphones, as she talks. Which capability fits?
notes.back: Speech translation.
notes.choices:
A) Language identification
B) Speech translation
C) Batch transcription
D) Text-to-speech avatar
notes.choicesExplained: A only names the language spoken. C transcribes stored audio later, in the same language. D turns text into a talking video.
notes.explanation: Speech translation handles real-time speech to speech translation of audio streams.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech translation?”, “What is speech translation?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The Speech service supports real-time, multi-language speech to speech and speech to text translation of audio streams.

notes.front: A news site wants a one-sentence description generated for every uploaded photo. Which Image Analysis feature fits?
notes.back: Captions.
notes.choices:
A) Tags
B) Captions
C) Object detection
D) Smart crop
notes.choicesExplained: A returns single-word labels, not sentences. C returns labels with coordinates. D returns a region for cropping.
notes.explanation: Captions describe an image in human-readable complete sentences.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Image Analysis?”, “Analyze Image” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Generate a caption of an image in human-readable language, using complete sentences.

notes.front: A stock photo library wants searchable keywords such as “beach”, “dog” and “outdoor” for each image; positions do not matter. Which feature fits?
notes.back: Tagging.
notes.choices:
A) Tagging
B) Object detection
C) Captions
D) OCR
notes.choicesExplained: B also returns coordinates, which are not needed. C writes sentences, not keywords. D reads text in the image.
notes.explanation: Tags label visual features, including the setting; the task needs no positions.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Image Analysis?”, “Analyze Image” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Identify and tag visual features in an image, from a set of thousands of recognizable objects, living things, scenery, and actions.

notes.front: A car park camera must report where each car is in the frame and how many there are. Which feature fits?
notes.back: Object detection.
notes.choices:
A) Tagging
B) Captions
C) Object detection
D) Smart crop
notes.choicesExplained: A says a car is present but not where. B describes the scene in a sentence. D picks one area of interest for cropping.
notes.explanation: Object detection returns a bounding box for each tagged object, including repeated instances.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Image Analysis?”, “Analyze Image” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: It also lets you know when there are multiple instances of the same tag in an image.

notes.front: An app must turn photos of handwritten shopping lists into editable text. Which capability fits?
notes.back: OCR with the Read engine.
notes.choices:
A) OCR with the Read engine
B) Image captions
C) Face detection
D) Image generation
notes.choicesExplained: B describes the picture, not the words written in it. C finds faces. D creates new images.
notes.explanation: Read extracts printed and handwritten text from images.
notes.source: Microsoft, “OCR - Optical Character Recognition”, “OCR engine” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: It extracts printed and handwritten text, including mixed languages and writing styles.

notes.front: A team is starting a five-year project that depends on Image Analysis 4.0. What should they note?
notes.back: It is deprecated and retires on 25 September 2028, after which calls fail.
notes.choices:
A) It is deprecated and retires on 25 September 2028, after which calls fail
B) It is the newest version and has no retirement date
C) It retired in 2025
D) It becomes free after 2028
notes.choicesExplained: B ignores the deprecation notice. C: the notice gives 2028, not 2025. D has no basis in the notice.
notes.explanation: The deprecation notice recommends switching to an alternative in the migration guide.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Image Analysis deprecation notice”, “Image Analysis deprecation notice” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: is deprecated and will be retired on September 25, 2028, after which calls made to the service will fail. We recommend you switch to one of the available alternatives

notes.front: A gym lets members in by looking at their face and finding them among all 3,000 members. Which operation is this?
notes.back: Face identification.
notes.choices:
A) Face verification
B) Face identification
C) Liveness detection
D) Face detection alone
notes.choicesExplained: A compares against one claimed identity. C checks the person is physically present. D only finds faces, not who they are.
notes.explanation: Identification matches one face against a set of faces: one-to-many.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is the Azure Face service?”, “Identification” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This scenario is used in granting building or airport access to a certain group of people or verifying the user of a device.

notes.front: A banking app compares a new selfie with the photo on the customer’s identity card. Which operation is this?
notes.back: Face verification.
notes.choices:
A) Face identification
B) Face verification
C) Face detection alone
D) OCR
notes.choicesExplained: A searches a whole set of faces. C does not compare faces. D reads the text on the card, not the face.
notes.explanation: Verification checks whether two faces belong to the same person: one-to-one.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is the Azure Face service?”, “Verification” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Verification can be used for access control, such as a banking app that enables users to open a credit account remotely by taking a new picture of themselves and sending it with a picture of their photo ID.

notes.front: A developer wants to verify a face but has only the raw image. What must the app call first?
notes.back: Face detection.
notes.choices:
A) Face detection
B) Liveness detection
C) Face identification
D) Nothing; verify accepts raw images only
notes.choicesExplained: B checks presence, not a prerequisite for every scenario. C is another recognition operation that also needs detection. D contradicts the rule that detection comes first.
notes.explanation: Detection returns the face identifier that the verify operation needs.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is the Azure Face service?”, “Face detection and analysis” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: It also returns a unique ID that represents the stored face data. This is used in later operations to identify or verify faces.

notes.front: Fraudsters try to pass a remote identity check by holding up a printed photo of the victim. Which feature counters this?
notes.back: Liveness detection.
notes.choices:
A) Face identification
B) Liveness detection
C) Face detection
D) Smart crop
notes.choicesExplained: A and C would happily match or find the face in the photo. D crops images.
notes.explanation: Liveness detection checks that a real person is physically present in front of the camera.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is the Azure Face service?”, “Example use cases” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: It's used to prevent spoofing attacks using a printed photo, recorded video, or a 3D mask of the user's face.

notes.front: A marketing team types “a red bicycle on a snowy mountain at dawn” and wants a new picture. Which capability fits?
notes.back: Image generation.
notes.choices:
A) Image Analysis
B) Image generation
C) Object detection
D) Captions
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D analyse images that already exist; none creates a new one.
notes.explanation: Image generation models create images from text prompts.
notes.source: Microsoft, “How to use image generation models from OpenAI”, “How to use image generation models from OpenAI” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: OpenAI's image generation models create images from user-provided text prompts and optional images.

notes.front: A firm wants the supplier, date and total pulled from thousands of scanned invoices into its finance system. Which workload is this?
notes.back: Intelligent document processing.
notes.choices:
A) Intelligent document processing
B) Image generation
C) Speech translation
D) Image tagging
notes.choicesExplained: B creates pictures. C translates speech. D labels what an image shows but does not pull out named fields.
notes.explanation: It converts unstructured documents into structured data, such as invoice fields.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools?”, “Content Understanding use cases” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For example, automate invoice processing, contract analysis, and claims management by extracting and validating fields from complex documents.

notes.front: A contact centre wants each recorded call turned into structured fields, such as the caller’s issue and outcome. Which workload is this?
notes.back: Information extraction.
notes.choices:
A) Speech synthesis
B) Information extraction
C) Pronunciation assessment
D) Image generation
notes.choicesExplained: A produces speech rather than reading it. C grades pronunciation. D creates images.
notes.explanation: It turns unstructured content, including audio, into a user-defined output format.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools?”, “What is Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: It uses generative AI to process and ingest many types of content, including documents, images, videos, and audio, into a user-defined output format.

notes.front: How does speech recognition differ from speech synthesis?
notes.back: Recognition turns spoken audio into text; synthesis turns text into spoken audio.
notes.explanation: They run in opposite directions, so the task’s input and output tell you which one you need.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Speech?”, “Capabilities” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use speech to text to convert audio into text.

notes.front: How does real-time transcription differ from batch transcription?
notes.back: Real-time transcribes live audio instantly with intermediate results; batch processes large volumes of stored audio asynchronously.
notes.explanation: Choose by whether someone needs the words now or a pile of recordings needs processing.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech to text?”, “Core features of speech to text” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Real-time transcription: Instant transcription with intermediate results for live audio inputs.

notes.front: How does object detection differ from tagging?
notes.back: Tagging returns labels; object detection also returns bounding box coordinates for each tagged object.
notes.explanation: Use detection when you need to know where things are, or how many there are.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Image Analysis?”, “Analyze Image” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Object detection is similar to tagging, but the API returns the bounding box coordinates for each tag applied.

notes.front: How does face verification differ from face identification?
notes.back: Verification is one-to-one: are these two faces the same person? Identification is one-to-many: who in this set is it?
notes.explanation: Verification confirms a claimed identity; identification searches a whole repository.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is the Azure Face service?”, “Face recognition operations” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Face verification ("one-to-one" matching) and Face identification ("one-to-many" matching)

notes.front: How does OCR differ from intelligent document processing?
notes.back: OCR extracts the text; IDP builds on OCR to extract structure, relationships, key-values and entities.
notes.explanation: IDP uses OCR as its foundational technology and adds document-centric insights on top.
notes.source: Microsoft, “OCR - Optical Character Recognition”, “How is OCR related to Intelligent Document Processing (IDP)?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Intelligent Document Processing (IDP) uses OCR as its foundational technology to extract structure, relationships, key-values, entities, and other document-centric insights

notes.front: How does computer vision differ from image generation?
notes.back: Computer vision analyses existing images and returns information; image generation creates new images from prompts.
notes.explanation: One reads pictures, the other makes them.
notes.source: Microsoft, “How to use image generation models from OpenAI”, “How to use image generation models from OpenAI” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: OpenAI's image generation models create images from user-provided text prompts and optional images.
